title: The Future of US-China Relations
gist: This is a promotional registration page for a 23 September 2026 Oxford Economics / Control Risks webinar, not an analytical piece: the only substantive signal is that Xi Jinping has a planned September visit to the United States, framed as a pivotal moment, and that Oxford Economics is pairing its trade/US/China economists with Control Risks geopolitical analysts to cover tariffs, technology restrictions and strategic rivalry. The adjacent webinar slate reveals the firm's live research agenda: China 'New New Three Industries', 'China shock 2.0' aimed at Europe, supply-chain chokepoints, an AI enterprise-spending wave, and Iran-war scenarios.

themes.theme: Xi's US visit as the pivot point

insights.claim: Chinese President Xi Jinping has a planned September 2026 visit to the United States, which Oxford Economics characterises as arriving at a pivotal moment for relations between the world's two largest economies.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: A head-of-state summit is the most likely near-term catalyst for tariff or export-control de-escalation headlines; position for event risk in China-exposed equities, semis and CNY around late September 2026.
insights.quote: President Xi Jinping’s planned September visit to the United States comes at a pivotal moment in relations between the world’s two largest economies.
insights.locator: President Xi Jinping's planned September visit

insights.claim: Oxford Economics frames the US-China relationship of recent years around exactly three dominant variables — tariffs, technology restrictions and strategic rivalry — rather than around trade balances or currency, implying policy tools rather than macro flows are the operative risk channel.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: Frame China exposure as a policy/regulatory risk book (entity lists, tariff schedules, licence regimes) rather than a cyclical demand call.
insights.quote: Tariffs, technology restrictions and strategic rivalry have dominated the relationship in recent years.
insights.locator: Tariffs, technology restrictions and strategic rivalry

themes.theme: Economics desks now buy geopolitical risk inputs

insights.claim: Oxford Economics is combining its Head of Global Trade, Chief US Economist and Chief China Economist with geopolitical and country-risk analysts from consultancy Control Risks in a single client session, a sign that macro forecasting houses no longer treat political risk as an exogenous add-on.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: Signals growing institutional demand (and budget) for geopolitical-risk consulting bundled into macro research — a structural tailwind for political-risk advisory providers.
insights.quote: Oxford Economics’ Head of Global Trade, Chief US Economist and Chief China Economist will be joined by geopolitical and country risk experts from Control Risks
insights.locator: To unpack where things stand and what may come next

insights.claim: Control Risks' North America practice defines its specialties as geopolitics, investment restrictions, sanctions and export controls, indicating that the client-side pain points for US-facing corporates are inbound/outbound investment screening and licensing rather than tariffs alone.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: Watch outbound-investment screening and export-control expansion as the binding constraint on US-China capital flows; it hits deal pipelines before it hits goods trade.
insights.quote: His specialties include geopolitics, investment restrictions, sanctions and export controls, as well as the evolving global economic, political, regulatory structures driving a shifting risk environment for companies.
insights.locator: Daniel Rechtschaffen is a Washington DC-based political

insights.claim: Oxford Economics has commercialised a dedicated global trade data platform called TradePrism, led out of Oxford Economics Australia, with research focused explicitly on the challenges and opportunities of economic decoupling.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: Trade-flow granularity is being productised; decoupling is now a monetisable data category, useful for tracking rerouting and transshipment in real time.
insights.quote: He leads the Australian Macroeconomic Service and global trade initiatives, including TradePrism.
insights.locator: Harry Murphy Cruise is the Head of Economic Research

themes.theme: Research agenda leaked by the adjacent webinar slate

insights.claim: Oxford Economics is running a 22 September 2026 session on the rise of China's 'New New Three Industries' asking 'Is this time any different?', implying the house view is that China's latest industrial-policy-led export champions may rhyme with the prior new-three (EVs, batteries, solar) overcapacity cycle.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: If the next wave repeats the overcapacity-then-price-collapse pattern, short the margin of the incumbent Western competitors in whichever sectors China designates next.
insights.quote: The Rise of the China ‘New New Three Industries’ – Is this time any different?

insights.claim: Oxford Economics has an on-demand product titled 'China shock 2.0: What is it and what can Europe do about it?', showing the firm treats Chinese export displacement primarily as a European policy problem rather than a purely US one.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: European trade-defence measures (anti-dumping, safeguard duties) are the under-priced leg of the tariff story relative to US headlines.
insights.quote: China shock 2.0: What is it and what can Europe do about it?

insights.claim: Oxford Economics treats supply-chain chokepoints as a standing analytic theme in their own right, with a session titled 'Trade under pressure: Chokepoints, geopolitical risk and global supply chains'.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: Chokepoint mapping (straits, single-source inputs, logistics nodes) is the practical lens for pricing tail risk in freight, insurance and inventory cycles.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics has published work sizing the uplift from an 'AI spending wave' to global enterprise tech budgets, indicating the firm models AI capex as a measurable macro-level enterprise budget shift rather than a vendor-specific story.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: A credible top-down enterprise-tech budget number is the cross-check on bottom-up AI revenue forecasts; divergence between the two is where the bubble debate gets resolved.
insights.quote: The AI spending wave: sizing the uplift to global enterprise tech budgets

insights.claim: Oxford Economics pairs AI growth and geopolitical uncertainty as a single navigation problem for Asia-Pacific industries in a 16 September 2026 session, suggesting the firm sees the AI buildout and the export-control regime as coupled rather than independent drivers for APAC.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: APAC hardware and semiconductor exposure should be stress-tested jointly against AI demand and licence-regime scenarios, not one at a time.
insights.quote: How can APAC Industries navigate AI growth and geopolitical uncertainty?

insights.claim: Oxford Economics maintains quantified global scenarios for the risks from the Iran war, showing the firm's macro framework now routinely carries live conflict scenarios alongside baseline forecasts.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: Scenario-weighted rather than point forecasts are the house standard; useful for stress-testing oil and inflation paths against conflict escalation.
insights.quote: Global scenarios – Quantifying the risks from the Iran war
